titles: 7 Best Budgeting Apps in 2026: Pricing, Pros and Cons
7 Best Budgeting Apps in 2026, Ranked by Who They Fit
Best Budgeting Apps in 2026: 7 Picks Compared
brief.metaDescription: Compare the 7 best budgeting apps in 2026 with pricing, pros, cons and who should skip each, so you can pick the one that fits how you spend.
brief.searchIntent: The searcher is ready to choose a budgeting app and wants a ranked shortlist with pricing, strengths, weak spots and who each app suits. A listicle with a comparison they can filter serves this best.
brief.reader: Adults in their 20s and 30s who want to get their spending under control. They know what a budget is, may have tried a spreadsheet or an app before, and want to pick one app today and start using it this week.
brief.angle: We rank each app by who it fits and say plainly who should skip it, instead of crowning one winner for everyone. We also explain that an app only helps when you use it, and we point to the no-app option and the safety checks.

outline.h2: How we picked these budgeting apps
points: Say plainly that this list draws on published tests and expert reviews and that we did not run our own hands-on test. Never claim 'we tested'.
Criteria, as a short list: bank connections that work, a number that tells you what you can safely spend, and early warnings about overspending (source 5).
Add consistency (an app you use beats an app with more features) and safety basics (source 4).
State that the order follows how often an app appears across the reviews we read and is never paid placement. Mention that Mint users moved to apps like Monarch after Mint shut down (source 4).

outline.h2: 1. Monarch Money: best for customizing your budget
points: What it does well: extensive customization, transaction tagging, recurring expense tracking, flexible budgeting and strong visual reports (source 4).
Source 5 calls it best for couples managing money together. Its budgeting style is flexible and it has debt payoff tools and rollover budgets (source 5).
Pricing: subscription required with no free version (source 4). The AI answers say about $99.99 per year with a 7-day free trial, so confirm on the Monarch site.
Pros: highly customizable, strong visual reports, a strong replacement for Mint (source 4). Con: predictive forecasts are limited (source 5).
Who should skip it: anyone who wants a free app or a very simple setup.

outline.h2: 2. YNAB: best for hands-on zero-based budgeting
points: What it does well: strict zero-based budgeting where every dollar gets a job. Source 5 names it best for hands-on budgeters. It has debt payoff tools and rollover budgets.
Pricing from the AI answers: $14.99 per month or $109 per year, with a 34-day free trial. Confirm on the YNAB site.
Pros: builds a regular habit and helps with paying down debt. Cons: zero-based only, so there is no other method to switch to, and predictive forecasts are limited (source 5).
Who should skip it: people who want an automatic, low-effort view of their money, since it asks you to assign funds regularly.

outline.h2: 3. PocketGuard: best for a safe-to-spend number
points: What it does well: it answers 'what can I safely spend right now?' after rent, bills and the savings goal you set. Source 5 highlights Leftover, Pace and monthly Insights.
It has over 1.7 million users on web, iOS and Android, according to source 5. Say this figure comes from that page.
Source 5's table shows multiple budgeting methods, predictive forecasts, debt payoff tools and rollover budgets. It is the only app in that table with a clear 'Yes' on forecasts.
Pricing is not in our sources, so the writer must send it to the editor to confirm and must not guess.
Who should skip it: people who want a free app or who prefer to plan on paper. Note that source 5 is a review site that ranks it first, so we present its praise as that site's view.

outline.h2: 4. Empower: best free app for the big picture
points: What it does well: one dashboard for checking, savings, investment and retirement accounts, plus retirement planning tools (source 4).
Pricing: completely free (source 4).
Pros: excellent account aggregation at no cost. Cons: fewer budgeting customization options and it lacks some spending alerts found in other apps (source 4).
Who should skip it: people who want detailed category budgets or alerts every time they overspend.

outline.h2: 5. Rocket Money: best for finding and cancelling subscriptions
points: What it does well: finds recurring subscriptions automatically, helps cancel the ones you no longer want, and can negotiate some monthly bills for you (source 4).
Pricing: a free version is available, but some premium features need an upgrade, and bill negotiation and cancellation may involve extra fees (source 4). Exact prices are not in our sources.
Source 5's table lists it for expense tracking only, with no predictive forecasts, no debt payoff tools and no rollover budgets.
Who should skip it: people who want a full budgeting system with forecasts or envelopes.

outline.h2: 6. Goodbudget: best for digital envelope budgeting
points: What it does well: it is a manual digital envelope system (source 5). You decide how much goes into each envelope and spend from it.
Source 5's table: envelope only, no predictive forecasts, limited debt payoff tools, rollover budgets yes.
Pricing from the AI answers: free and Plus plans, with Plus at $8 per month or $70 per year. Confirm on the Goodbudget site.
Pros: a clear method if you like putting a limit on each category. Con: manual, so you enter spending yourself.
Who should skip it: people who want automatic bank syncing to do the work.

outline.h2: 7. EveryDollar: best for Ramsey-style monthly budgets
points: What it does well: zero-based monthly budgets in the Ramsey style (source 5).
Source 5's table: no predictive forecasts, limited debt payoff tools, limited rollover budgets.
Pricing from the AI Overview: a simple free tier, with bank syncing needing a paid upgrade. Confirm on the EveryDollar site.
Who should skip it: people who want automatic bank syncing for free or who prefer a flexible method.

outline.h2: How to choose the right budgeting app for you
points: Start with the job you need done: subscriptions (Rocket Money), a free overview (Empower), customization (Monarch), a strict plan (YNAB), a safe-to-spend number (PocketGuard), envelopes (Goodbudget) or a monthly Ramsey-style plan (EveryDollar) (sources 4, 5).
An app will not fix spending habits. It shows where your money goes so you can make choices, and consistency matters most (source 4).

A spreadsheet is a fair option too. The Asti Financial planner still uses Excel after 35 years in planning (source 4). Ramit Sethi's Conscious Spending Plan is another way to manage money without strict budgeting (source 2).
Give the safety checks: bank-level encryption, two-factor authentication and read-only access, which lets an app show your accounts but never move money (source 4).
Point readers to our budget calculator to set a monthly number before picking an app.

h3.title: Check safety first
points: Use a list of the three checks above and explain read-only access in one sentence.

h3.title: Pick one and give it a month
points: Suggest choosing one app, linking accounts and reviewing spending weekly, then switching if it does not fit.

gaps: Source 4 covers only three apps and gives no pricing. Source 5 compares six but its excerpt gives no pricing and it ranks its own favorite first. We give pricing for each app, with a note to confirm it.
Neither page says clearly who should skip each app. We add a 'who should skip it' point for every option.
Several top Google results for this keyword are not about budgeting apps: an investing hub, a personal finance course homepage and a deals page. A direct ranked comparison serves the searcher better.
Safety gets one line in the sources. We explain the three checks and what read-only access means.
Few pages say that a spreadsheet or no app is a fair choice, or link the app choice to setting a monthly number first.

faqs.question: What is the best app for planning monthly budgets?
faqs.answer: It depends on your style. Say EveryDollar suits zero-based monthly plans, YNAB suits hands-on zero-based budgeting, and Monarch suits flexible budgets (sources 4, 5).

faqs.question: What is Dave Ramsey's favorite budget app?
faqs.answer: Say we cannot speak for Ramsey. Source 5 names EveryDollar as best for Ramsey-style monthly budgets, and it uses a zero-based monthly method.

faqs.question: Are budgeting apps safe?
faqs.answer: Generally yes with a reputable company. Look for bank-level encryption, two-factor authentication and read-only access, which cannot move money (source 4).

faqs.question: Do I need a budgeting app at all?
faqs.answer: No. A spreadsheet, notebook or app all work if you use them consistently, and an app will not fix spending habits by itself (source 4).

faqs.question: Is there a free budgeting app?
faqs.answer: Empower is completely free, and Rocket Money has a free version with paid extras (source 4). The AI Overview says EveryDollar has a free tier, so confirm that.

blocks.text: Picking a budgeting app is easier when you know what you need it to do, because a balance alone can't tell you what bills are coming.
In this guide, we rank seven apps by who each one fits, with pricing notes, strengths and weak spots. We also say plainly who should skip each one, because no single app suits everyone.
By the end, you'll be able to pick one app today and start using it this week.

sections.h2: How we picked these budgeting apps

blocks.text: This list draws on published tests and expert reviews, and we did not run our own hands-on test of these apps. We read what other reviewers found, then ranked each app by who it fits. For more on the basics behind the choices, see our [money basics](https://clearmoney.example/blog/money-basics) guide.
Here's what we looked for, based on what [one review site](https://bestmobileappawards.com/blog/top-rated-mobile-apps-for-budgeting-2026) says makes a budgeting app stand out:

items: Bank connections that work, so you don't have to type in every coffee by hand.
A number that tells you what you can safely spend after rent, bills and savings goals.
Early warnings about overspending, so you can spot patterns and act on your pace.

blocks.text: We added two more checks. The first is consistency, because as one financial planner puts it, [consistency matters far more than technology](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day), so an app you use beats an app with more features. The second is safety basics, which we cover near the end of this guide.

We ordered the list by who each app fits best, and no app paid for its spot. Luckily, one detail from our reading is easy to share, since many people who used Mint [moved to apps like Monarch](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day) after Mint shut down.

sections.h2: 1. Monarch Money: best for customizing your budget

blocks.text: Monarch Money is a budgeting app that connects to your accounts and lets you organize your spending in a way that suits you.
One financial planner says it offers extensive customization, transaction tagging, recurring expense tracking and budgeting flexibility.
Here's how the pros and cons stack up from those reviews:

items: It is [highly customizable](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day), so you can shape your budget around your own habits.
It has excellent visual reports, according to the same planner.
It is a strong replacement for Mint, which is why many former Mint users moved to it.
Its predictive forecasts are [limited](https://bestmobileappawards.com/blog/top-rated-mobile-apps-for-budgeting-2026), so it won't warn you about what's coming as well as some other apps.

blocks.text: Monarch Money requires a subscription and has [no free version](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day). The AI answers we checked say it costs about $99.99 per year with a 7-day free trial, so confirm the current price on the Monarch site before you sign up.
Who should skip it: anyone who wants a free app or a very simple setup, since the extra customization is most useful if you enjoy tuning your budget.

sections.h2: 2. YNAB: best for hands-on zero-based budgeting

blocks.text: YNAB (You Need A Budget) is a budgeting app that uses **zero-based budgeting**, which means you give every dollar you earn a job before you spend it. [Best Mobile App Awards](https://bestmobileappawards.com/blog/top-rated-mobile-apps-for-budgeting-2026) names it best for hands-on budgeters, and its table lists debt payoff tools and rollover budgets.
If you like having a plan for each paycheck, this is the app that asks the most of you in return, and that regular effort is where its benefits come from.
The AI answers we checked list the price at $14.99 per month or $109 per year, with a 34-day free trial. Please confirm the current price on the YNAB site before you sign up.
Here are the pros and cons from the reviews we read:

items: It includes debt payoff tools and rollover budgets, which can help if you're [paying down debt](https://clearmoney.example/credit).
It uses zero-based budgeting only, so there is no other method to switch to if that style stops fitting your life.

Its predictive forecasts are limited, according to [the comparison table](https://bestmobileappawards.com/blog/top-rated-mobile-apps-for-budgeting-2026), so it won't warn you about upcoming bills as well as some other apps.

blocks.text: Who should skip it: people who want an automatic, low-effort view of their money, since YNAB asks you to assign funds on a regular basis. Honestly, if you know you won't open an app a few times a week, one of the lighter options below will suit you better.

sections.h2: 3. PocketGuard: best for a safe-to-spend number

blocks.text: It works that out after your rent, bills and the savings goal you set, so you don't have to do the math at the register.
We're describing them as that review site does, since we haven't tested the app ourselves.

items: Leftover shows what's safe to spend after your bills and savings goal.
Pace shows where your spending is heading, so you can slow down before you overspend.
Insights and monthly reviews help you spot patterns in how you spend.

blocks.text: According to [that same page](https://bestmobileappawards.com/blog/top-rated-mobile-apps-for-budgeting-2026), PocketGuard has over 1.7 million users on web, iOS and Android. Its comparison table lists multiple budgeting methods, debt payoff tools and rollover budgets.
Our sources don't give a price for PocketGuard, so please check the current cost on the PocketGuard site before you sign up. We've also asked our editor to confirm it for this guide.
Keep in mind that the review site that praises PocketGuard also ranks it first, so treat that praise as one site's view.
Who should skip it: people who want a free app, or who would rather plan their month on paper. If you like writing every dollar down yourself, a spreadsheet may suit you better.

sections.h2: 4. Empower: best free app for the big picture

blocks.text: Empower is a personal finance app that pulls all your accounts into one dashboard, and [according to Asti Financial](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day) it is completely free. If you want a simple way to see where you stand without paying a monthly fee, it's worth a look.
You can view your checking, savings, investment and retirement accounts all in one place, and the app also includes retirement planning tools, as that same review points out.
Here's what Asti Financial's review says you get and what you give up:

items: You get excellent **account aggregation** at no cost, so every balance sits on one screen.
You get retirement planning tools alongside your everyday accounts.
You give up some budgeting customization, since the app has fewer options than others on this list.
You give up some spending alerts that other apps include.

blocks.text: For many people this works as a way to understand their overall financial picture, which is how the reviewer describes it for their own clients.
Who should skip it: people who want detailed category budgets, or an alert every time they overspend. If that's you, Monarch Money or PocketGuard will give you more control.
Empower makes a good first app if you're not sure how much hands-on budgeting you want.

sections.h2: 5. Rocket Money: best for finding and cancelling subscriptions

blocks.text: Rocket Money is a personal finance app that finds your recurring subscriptions, helps you cancel the ones you no longer want and can negotiate some of your monthly bills.
Here's what the review says it does well:

items: It identifies your recurring subscriptions automatically, so you don't have to hunt through statements.
It helps you cancel the subscriptions you no longer want.
It can negotiate certain monthly bills on your behalf.
It has an easy-to-use interface and a free version.

blocks.text: Pricing is where you'll want to read the fine print. The same review says some premium features require an upgrade, and bill negotiation and subscription cancellation may involve additional fees.
Our sources don't list exact prices, so check Rocket Money's own site before you sign up.

On features, [the comparison table at Best Mobile App Awards](https://bestmobileappawards.com/blog/top-rated-mobile-apps-for-budgeting-2026) lists Rocket Money for expense tracking. That table shows no predictive forecasts, no debt payoff tools and no rollover budgets, which tells you where its strengths stop.
Who should skip it: people who want a full budgeting system with forecasts, rollover budgets or envelopes. If you want to plan every dollar ahead of time, YNAB or Goodbudget will fit better.
You can pair it with a different app for your day-to-day plan.

sections.h2: 6. Goodbudget: best for digital envelope budgeting

blocks.text: Goodbudget is a budgeting app that uses a **digital envelope** system, where you set aside money for each spending category and spend only from that envelope. According to [Best Mobile App Awards](https://bestmobileappawards.com/blog/top-rated-mobile-apps-for-budgeting-2026), it is a manual system, so you decide how much goes into each envelope and you enter your spending yourself.
If you like the idea of a hard limit on groceries or eating out, this is a clear way to get it.
Here's how the same review's comparison table describes it:

items: Its budgeting style is envelope only, so there is no other method to switch to.
It has no predictive forecasts.
Its debt payoff tools are limited.
It does support rollover budgets, so unspent money can carry into the next period.

blocks.text: On pricing, the AI answers we reviewed say Goodbudget has a free plan and a Plus plan at $8 per month or $70 per year. Please confirm those numbers on the Goodbudget site before you sign up, since our sources don't list them directly.
What works: a simple, visible limit on each category.

Who should skip it: people who want automatic bank syncing to do the work. If you know you won't log purchases by hand, an app that pulls in transactions for you, like Monarch Money or Rocket Money, will suit you better.

sections.h2: 7. EveryDollar: best for Ramsey-style monthly budgets

blocks.text: EveryDollar is a budgeting app that builds a zero-based monthly budget in the Ramsey style.
If you like to sit down at the start of each month and plan your spending line by line, this style may feel natural to you.
Here's how the same review's comparison table describes it:

items: Its budgeting style is zero-based and monthly.
Its debt payoff tools are limited.
Its rollover budgets are limited, so unspent money may not carry over as easily as in some other apps.

blocks.text: On pricing, the Google AI Overview we reviewed says EveryDollar has a simple free tier for zero-based budgeting, while bank syncing needs a paid upgrade. Please confirm the current plans and prices on the EveryDollar site before you sign up, since our sources don't list them directly.
What works: a simple monthly plan that is easy to read.

Who should skip it: people who want automatic bank syncing for free, or who prefer a flexible method over a strict monthly plan. If that sounds like you, Empower is free and pulls in your accounts, and Monarch Money offers a more flexible budgeting style.

sections.h2: How to choose the right budgeting app for you

items: If you want to find and cancel recurring subscriptions, Rocket Money is built for that, according to [Asti Financial](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day).

If you want a free overview of every account in one place, Empower fits that need, as [Asti Financial](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day) describes it.
If you like to organize your budget your own way, Monarch Money offers extensive customization, per the same review.
If you want a number that shows what you can safely spend, PocketGuard is that review's pick.
If you like limits on each category, Goodbudget uses digital envelopes.
If you want a monthly Ramsey-style plan, EveryDollar offers one.

blocks.text: Luckily, you don't need an app to fix every spending habit, and none of them can do it alone. [Asti Financial](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day) says an app is simply a tool for seeing where your money goes so you can make choices, and that consistency matters far more than technology.

That also means a spreadsheet is a fair option. The Asti Financial planner still uses Excel after more than 35 years in financial planning, and [Ramit Sethi's Conscious Spending Plan](https://www.iwillteachyoutoberich.com/) is another way to manage money without strict budgeting.
Check safety first

Before you link a bank account, look for these three things, which [Asti Financial](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day) lists as features to look for in a reputable app:

items: The app uses bank-level encryption.
The app offers two-factor authentication.
The app asks for read-only access to your accounts.

blocks.text: Read-only access means the app can show your account information but cannot move money or make transactions.
Pick one and give it a month

Choose one app, link your accounts and review your spending once a week. If it does not fit after a month, switch to another app on this list, since the right match depends on how you like to work. For more help, see [our budgeting guides](https://clearmoney.example/budgeting).

Not sure what monthly number to start with? Try our [Clear Money budget calculator](https://clearmoney.example/tools/budget-calculator), then pick the app from this list that fits it and give it a month.
What is the best app for planning monthly budgets?
Here is how the apps fit different needs:

items: [Bestmobileappawards.com](https://bestmobileappawards.com/blog/top-rated-mobile-apps-for-budgeting-2026) lists EveryDollar as best for Ramsey-style zero-based monthly budgets.
[Bestmobileappawards.com](https://bestmobileappawards.com/blog/top-rated-mobile-apps-for-budgeting-2026) lists YNAB as best for hands-on zero-based budgeting.
Asti Financial describes Monarch as a good fit if you want a highly customizable, flexible system.

blocks.text: What is Dave Ramsey's favorite budget app?
It uses a zero-based monthly method where you plan every dollar of your income.
Are budgeting apps safe?

Generally yes, as long as you use a reputable company, according to [Asti Financial](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day). Look for these three safety checks:

items: Bank-level encryption.
Two-factor authentication.
Read-only access, which lets an app show your account information without being able to move money.

blocks.text: Do I need a budgeting app at all?

No. A spreadsheet, a notebook or an app can all work if you use them consistently, and [Asti Financial](https://astifinancial.com/the-best-budgeting-apps-of-2026-and-the-one-i-still-use-every-day) notes that an app will not fix spending habits on its own. The best choice is the one you will actually open each week.
Is there a free budgeting app?
Yes.
Google's AI Overview says EveryDollar has a free tier with bank syncing on a paid plan, so confirm that on the EveryDollar site before you rely on it.
